title: How Good Is The Cheapest X-LAB Road Bike?

takeaways.text: CADE weighed the size S RS5 five times without pedals: 9.35 kg, with Shimano 105 mechanical, Branta alloy wheels and 32 mm tyres.
The geometry puts the bars a little higher and closer than on a race bike. X-LAB calls it true endurance geometry, but CADE found it not as short or tall as a Specialized Roubaix or Pinarello X.
One model at one price, US$1,399, sold through X-LAB's US offices and dealers at publication, while a European network was still being set up; CADE compared it with Canyon's Endurace AllRoad.

The aluminium frame did not feel harsh on the grippy 32 mm Branta slicks, and 38 mm clearance leaves room for wider tyres. CADE sees it as a training, touring or commuting bike, with rack and mudguard mounts.
Neither the wheels nor the tyres are tubeless-ready. X-LAB said a future update might add tubeless wheels but did not say whether or when.

Five sizes, XS to XL. CADE found no size small enough for many shorter riders: two riders just under average women's height would be uncomfortable on the XS, whose bars would be 4 cm too wide for them.

Unlike X-LAB's top models there is no free component swap. The alloy one-piece cockpit costs US$375 to replace, and its internally routed mechanical cables and hoses make changing it or lowering the stem a costly faff.

The box-fresh frame had small paint defects around the headset showing the white undercoat; bolts, threads and thru-axles felt high quality. The box included a bottle cage, a light, a torque wrench, tools and a computer mount.

disclosure: CADE Media says it was not paid and X-LAB had no say in the video; the bike arrived box-fresh for the review. The description names Garmin as a channel sponsor.
summary: An October 2026 first look at the US$1,399 aluminium X-LAB RS5 in size S with Shimano 105 mechanical, a Branta power-meter crank and 32 mm tyres, covering a weigh-in, sizing, tubeless limits, the one-piece cockpit and routing, and the finish.
